Business plan text:

Drafty
Drafty Executive Summary
Problem
Every winter, millions of renters open a utility bill that is far higher than expected and have
no idea why. In older multifamily buildings, a large share of heating energy is lost through
leaky windows, gaps under doors, unsealed outlets and poorly insulated walls. Renters usually
pay the utility bill but do not own the building, so they are stuck. A professional energy
audit typically costs several hundred dollars, is designed for homeowners, and often ends in a
report that recommends upgrades a tenant cannot make. Small landlords, who own most rental
units in the country, have the opposite problem: they are responsible for the building but
rarely see the bills, so they have little data and little motivation to act.
We saw this ourselves. In a survey of 212 students and young renters at our university and
nearby neighborhoods, 78 percent said their winter heating costs were higher than expected, and
only 9 percent could name the cause. Residential energy costs also keep rising, which makes the
problem sharper each year. The result is wasted money, wasted energy and avoidable emissions,
with no simple tool to fix it.
Solution
Drafty is a sensor-and-app kit that maps heat loss in an apartment and tells the user what to
fix first. Each kit has six small wireless sensors that measure temperature, humidity and air
movement. The user places them at windows, doors, outlets and baseboards for about 48 hours and
pairs them with the app. Our software combines the readings with outdoor weather and basic
details about the unit, then produces a heat-loss map and a ranked list of fixes sorted by
cost, effort and estimated payback.
Most recommended fixes cost under 40 dollars and need no contractor or permission:
weatherstripping, door sweeps, outlet gaskets, window film, curtain changes. The app links to
the parts and gives short installation guides. After fixes are made, users can rerun the
sensors to see measured improvement, which is what makes Drafty different from a generic
checklist. Landlords can also use a portfolio dashboard to compare units and prioritize
repairs.
Market
The United States has about 44 million renter households. Most pay at least part of their own
energy costs. We focus first on renters in older multifamily buildings in cold and mixed
climates, roughly 12 million households. If a quarter of them bought one kit at our planned
price, the one-time hardware market alone would be above 100 million dollars, before recurring
landlord subscriptions. The second segment is small landlords, owners of one to twenty units,
who hold a large share of rental housing and are underserved by existing energy tools. We
estimate about 2 million such owners nationwide.
A third, longer-term segment is utilities and city energy programs, which are required in many
states to meet efficiency targets and pay for measurable savings. Our anonymized data on where
homes lose heat is valuable to them.
Business Model
We earn money in three ways. First, we sell the sensor kit directly to renters for 59 dollars.
Our current cost of goods is about 24 dollars per kit at small volume, and we expect it to fall
below 18 dollars when we order at scale. Second, we sell a landlord subscription at 6 dollars
per unit per month, which includes the portfolio dashboard, repeat scans each season and a
prioritized repair plan. Third, we plan to license anonymized, aggregated building data to
utilities and efficiency programs. Affiliate revenue from recommended parts adds a small
additional margin.

Sensors are reusable, so a single kit can be lent between units or reused each year, which
lowers the cost for landlords and keeps subscription customers engaged.
Competition
Our competitors fall into three groups. Professional energy auditors give detailed results but
cost hundreds of dollars and serve homeowners. Smart thermostats and general home sensors
collect data but do not diagnose heat loss or recommend fixes. Free online checklists and
utility tips are cheap but generic and do not tell a renter what is wrong in their particular
apartment. Thermal-camera attachments for phones exist, but they need skill to interpret and
only show surface temperature at one moment.
Drafty is built for renters and small landlords, costs a fraction of an audit, and gives a
ranked, apartment-specific action list with measured before-and-after results. Our advantage is
the combination of low-cost hardware with analysis software, and the data we collect with every
scan will make our recommendations more accurate over time.
Team
Maya Okonkwo-Reyes, our CEO, is a senior in environmental policy who ran the renter survey and
leads customer development and partnerships. Daniel Whitfield, our CTO, is a senior in
electrical engineering who designed the sensor hardware and firmware. Priyanka Venkataraman,
our head of data, is a master's student in data science who built the heat-loss model and the
ranking engine. Tomas Brandt, our head of product, is a junior in industrial design who leads
the app and kit design. We are advised by a faculty member in building energy systems and a
retired property manager with thirty years of experience in small multifamily buildings.
Milestones and Financials
We have defined the core concept, built a working prototype of the kit and app, and put it in
front of outside users. Over the last winter we ran Drafty in 41 apartments. Of these, 27 users
paid for the kit at a discounted pilot price, and one local property manager with 60 units
signed a paid pilot for 12 units. In follow-up scans, users who completed at least three
recommended fixes measured an average 14 percent reduction in temperature loss at problem
points, and self-reported bills dropped by an estimated 8 to 12 percent. Our app is live and
our website collects signups, with a waitlist of over 400 people.
We have not yet formed a legal entity and plan to incorporate in the coming months. To date we
have spent about 9,000 dollars, mostly on parts and prototypes, funded by pilot revenue and a
small university grant. Pilot revenue so far is about 2,300 dollars. We project 85,000 dollars
in revenue in the first full year, mostly from kit sales and landlord pilots, rising to roughly
420,000 dollars in year two as subscriptions grow and we add our first utility data pilot.
What We Are Asking For
We are seeking 40,000 dollars in prize or seed funding. About half would go to our first
production run of 800 kits and certification testing, 30 percent to app development and our
data pipeline, and the rest to legal formation, insurance and marketing to landlords. Beyond
funding, we would value introductions to property management associations, utility program
contacts and mentors with hardware manufacturing experience. With this support we expect to
complete incorporation, double our landlord pilots, and be ready for a public launch ahead of
next winter.

Question: Comment on the viability and scalability of the business model and strategy. Address whether the company has a clear path to making money and growing, and evaluate the validity of the entrepreneur's assumptions.

response.text:
The business model and strategy of Drafty show a clear path to monetization and scalability, but the viability and growth potential depend on several critical assumptions and execution factors.

**Viability of the Business Model:**
- **Revenue Streams:** Drafty has three revenue streams: sensor kits, landlord subscriptions, and data licensing. These are well-structured and align with the target market segments (renters, small landlords, utilities). The sensor kit is a one-time purchase, and the subscription model provides recurring revenue, which is essential for long-term sustainability.
- **Pricing and Margins:** The pricing of the sensor kit at $59 is competitive relative to professional energy audits, and the cost of goods is expected to decrease with scale. The subscription model at $6/unit/month is reasonable for the value provided (dashboard, repeat scans, repair plans). The data licensing revenue is a promising long-term opportunity but depends on building relationships with utilities and efficiency programs.
- **Scalability:** The reusable nature of the sensors allows for cost-effective scaling, as a single kit can be used across multiple units or years. This reduces the hardware cost per user and supports a scalable business model.

**Scalability of the Strategy:**
- **Market Size:** The target market of 12 million renters in older multifamily buildings and 2 million small landlords is substantial. The potential revenue from a quarter of these users (around $100 million for kits alone) is compelling, especially if the product gains traction.
- **Differentiation:** Drafty differentiates itself by providing actionable, apartment-specific recommendations with measurable results. This is a key advantage over generic checklists or smart thermostats that do not address heat loss directly.
- **Data Feedback Loop:** The data collected from each scan improves the accuracy of the heat-loss model over time, which enhances the product's value and supports long-term growth.

**Assumptions and Validity:**
- **User Adoption:** The assumption that 25% of targeted renters will purchase a kit is optimistic. The current waitlist of 400 people is a positive sign, but scaling to 12 million households requires significant marketing and distribution efforts.
- **Landlord Engagement:** The success of the landlord subscription model depends on convincing small landlords to adopt the product. The current pilot with one property manager is a start, but broader adoption will require demonstrating ROI and ease of use.
- **Cost Reduction:** The assumption that COGS will fall below $18 per kit at scale is critical. If production costs remain high, the margin on sensor kits could be too narrow to support growth.
- **Regulatory and Data Access:** Licensing data to utilities and efficiency programs depends on regulatory compliance and data privacy standards. The company must navigate these hurdles effectively.

**Conclusion:**
Drafty has a viable and scalable business model with clear revenue streams and a differentiated value proposition. However, the success of the strategy hinges on the validity of key assumptions, particularly around user adoption, cost reduction, and regulatory compliance. The company must execute on marketing, distribution, and product refinement to realize its growth potential. The proposed funding request is reasonable for the next phase of development and scaling, but the team must demonstrate strong traction and a clear path to profitability.
